newsitem.title: THAILAND: Hopewell's Wu seeks Thai help for Bangkok project.
newsitem.headline: Hopewell's Wu seeks Thai help for Bangkok project.

text.p: Hong Kong's Hopewell Holdings on Friday sought Thai help to secure loans and submitted an eight-point proposal to speed up building of its delayed $3.2 billion Bangkok rail and highway transit system.
Visiting Hopewell chairman Gordon Wu also sought assurances from government officials that a 30-year concession obtained six years ago by his firm to build the system would not be revoked.

Wu asked for government help in securing 2.5 billion baht ($100 million) in local commercial loans which, he said, would boost the confidence of Hopewell's foreign creditors and enable them to provide additional financing for the project.

Thai Transport and Communications Minister Suwat Liptapallop, who was briefed by Wu on the project's progress, told reporters he had asked Hopewell to give legally binding assurances that the system would be completed on schedule.
Suwat said Hopewell and Thai officials would meet next week to review Wu's proposals. He said the government would also ask the company to detail its plans for securing local and foreign financing.
A defiant Wu on Friday dismissed concerns that his project, expected to help partly solve Bangkok's chronic traffic congestion, faced major construction delays.
"What delay? There is no delay. The project will be finished before the (1998) Asian Games. Don't listen to other people," Wu told Reuters after meeting Suwat.
The Hong Kong magnate in the past has blamed Thai red tape in approving specifications for the multi-level rail and highway system for delays.
Suwat said less than 20 percent of the 60-km (35-mile) system had been completed.
Hopewell was required to finish at least two thirds of the system on the northern and eastern Bangkok routes by December 1998, in time for the Asian Games to be held in the capital.
Thai officials estimated that Hopewell had invested about 12 billion baht, mostly in piling works on the system's northern route.
They said the company needed to spend another 20 billion baht on civic and structural construction and another 30 billion baht on rail, rolling stock and other equipment.

Hopewell, which posted a fiscal 1996 net profit of HK$769 million against HK$2.1 billion a year earlier, last October trimmed its corporate debt by selling a large portion of its stake in Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd (CEPA)
Wu also sought government approval for an early opening of the northern and eastern routes and assurances that highway tolls and train fares would be allowed to rise in line with inflation.
Wu asked Suwat to postpone until September a schedule for Hopewell to raise its operating capital to 30 billion baht from the current 12 billion.
Hopewell was earlier expected to boost the capital by the first quarter of this year after the sale of its stake in CEPA.
